items.content:
The executive meeting does not rescue a weak S&OP cycle. It exposes where the hand-offs stopped.

Once Operations reopens the capacity assumptions, Finance starts rebuilding the gap to plan, and Commercial explains what moved, the meeting is no longer choosing between prepared options. It is reconstructing the pre-work with the executive team already in the room.

Where I think the process often breaks is in the hand-off between reviews. A review can happen on time, use the right template, and still leave the next team with work it cannot use.

The data can be accurate, but the exceptions may have no owner. Demand can agree a number that has not been tested against supply. Supply can produce feasible options without showing the service or financial consequence. Integrated reconciliation can quantify the gap and still arrive without a recommendation.

In each case, the review happened but the actual hand-off did not.

The exact review names and ownership will vary between businesses, but the operating test is useful: each review should remove avoidable uncertainty from the next decision.

Before an unresolved issue enters the meeting, I would want four things visible:

• Evidence: what changed, and what do we trust?
• Owner: who is accountable for moving it?
• Options: what can the business genuinely choose?
• Ask: what decision requires executive authority?

Think about your last executive S&OP: which discussion arrived with a well-described problem, but no choice the room could actually make?

items.content:
The best supply chains do not avoid every disruption. They respond faster because the rhythm is already clear. 

Because in the actual moment, the team is not asking whether resilience is important. Everyone already knows it is important. The question is much more practical:

What do we look at first, who needs to decide, what options do we really have, and how quickly can we recover flow?

That is where most companies get exposed.

They may have the risk register. They may have the dashboard. They may even have extra inventory sitting somewhere in the network. But if the team does not have a shared way to read the situation and choose the next move, the response still becomes a chain of escalations.

For me, a stronger resilience conversation looks at the full operating system:
• What signal are we trusting?
• What capacity assumption just changed?
• Which supplier or route gives us optionality?
• Where is the bottleneck now?
• How long can we survive, and how long will recovery take?
• What rule needs to change so this does not become the same fire drill next quarter?

The best supply chains are not the ones that avoid every problem. They are the ones that respond with less confusion, recover with more discipline, and then improve because of what the disruption exposed.

Which part of this operating system would fail first in your supply chain?

items.content:
Everyone reinforces the wrong clause.

When a supply contract hits the negotiation table, most of the energy goes to one thing: liability. 

Who pays when something goes wrong. It has been the single most-negotiated term in commercial contracts since 2007, and that makes sense, because nobody wants to be the one left holding the bill.

This is Episode 35 of Supply Chain 101, where I break down one supply chain idea at a time, in plain language, for people inside the field and outside it.

A supply contract really rests on six clauses, not one:
• Price and indexation: what you pay, and how that price is allowed to move.
• Scope and specification: what you actually agreed to deliver.
• Delivery and lead time: when and how it shows up.
• Quality and SLA: the standard it has to meet.
• Liability and remedies: who carries the risk when it breaks.
• Term and exit: how the relationship starts, and how it ends.

And here is the twist. 77% of contract disputes do not start at liability at all. 

They start at scope, the clause about what was actually promised, because two parties read the same words and walked away with two different pictures of the job.

So teams armour the clause that rarely cracks, and leave the one that quietly does the most damage half-defined.

My view on this is that a contract is not won in the clause you argue hardest. It is won in the clause you make impossible to misread.

Which clause in your last supplier contract turned out to be the one nobody could agree on afterwards?

items.content:
Who carries the cost when the work runs over?

This week on Supply Chain 101 we are staying inside the contract on episode 36. 

The earlier post looked at what actually lives in one. This one is about how it is priced, because once the clauses are set, the pricing model is what quietly decides who absorbs the risk when costs move.

Here is the simple version. Imagine the same job, agreed at the same number, hit by the same surprise: it runs over budget. Three contracts, three very different outcomes.

• Fixed-Price: you agree one number up front and the supplier delivers for that, whatever happens. If costs rise, the supplier absorbs it, and you pay for that safety in a premium baked into the price from day one.
• Time and Materials: you pay for the hours worked and the materials used. When the job runs long, the bill grows with it, so the risk is shared, but it leans toward you.
• Cost-Plus: you reimburse the supplier’s actual costs and add an agreed fee on top. If the work overruns, you carry it, and the supplier still earns their margin.

The lowest number on paper is often the one that quietly hands you all the risk.

So if a key supplier contract ran 20% over next quarter, which pricing model are you on, and would that surprise land on you or on them?

items.content:
Your supplier's price increase lands on your desk 48 hours before the meeting. How much of it can they actually justify?

Most category managers walk in with last year's price and a margin assumption from memory. The actual cost build stays on their side of the table: raw materials, labour, overhead, and the margin layer sitting on top of all of it. The negotiation opens with their number and you respond to it.

A should-cost model changes that

Last week, we reviewed we broke down the RFQ on episode 27, now we focus on cost modeling. You give ChatGPT the product specs, the bill of materials in whatever form you have, and the key cost drivers. ChatGPT structures the cost model: separates the four layers, sizes each one proportionally, and returns a should-cost range with the margin layer visible. 

Now you know which layers are structural (commodity costs, labour rates, fixed overhead) and which one you can actually move.

How to do it:
• Open ChatGPT. Paste your product specs and any BOM data you have.
• Prompt: "Build a should-cost model for [product]. Components: [list]. Key drivers: [materials, labour region, annual volume]. Show each cost layer as a percentage of total and as an absolute value. Where does supplier margin typically sit in this category?"
• Cross-reference the output against any commodity data you have. Adjust one assumption. You have a credible anchor.
• Walk into the meeting with it.

ChatGPT works here because this is a structuring and calculation task: multiple input types, proportional cost layers, margin separated out.

And one honest limitation: if the product has proprietary inputs the supplier will not disclose, the model becomes directional rather than precise. Use it to anchor the conversation, not to challenge line by line.

What you get: a cost breakdown by layer with percentages and a should-cost range, ready before they present their number.

Try this before your next supplier price review.

items.content:
The closer a requirement gets to the factory, the more expensive a casual change becomes.

That is why I find it useful to think about the Master Production Schedule as the line between planning intent and factory commitment.

At forecast level, a new signal is information. Inside the near-term production horizon, the same signal may require material checks, rough-cut capacity review, changes to planned or released orders, and a decision about which customer commitment the team is still protecting.

A stronger MPS review makes four things explicit:
• which item is affected
• what quantity is moving
• which period changes
• whether the line is planned, firm, or already released 
And then it applies a different level of control depending on where the change sits.

Firming converts planned orders into actual production or purchase orders. The exact configuration will vary between systems and businesses, but the operating principle is the same: the closer the plan gets to execution, the more deliberate the change needs to become.

The MPS is not the detailed production sequence either, it does not decide every machine slot or changeover. It creates the item-time commitment that material planning, capacity checks, production orders, and detailed scheduling can work from.

So when demand moves, the useful conversation is not only “can we change the plan?”
It is:
• What exactly are we changing?
• What has already been protected or firmed?
• Which material, capacity, order, or customer commitment moves with it?
• Who owns the exception? 

Protected does not mean impossible to change, it means the business understands that responsiveness has a cost, and the trade-off should be visible before the schedule moves.

When demand changes inside your near-term horizon, who owns the decision to change the MPS?

---

items.content:
Excel can calculate EOQ, but ChatGPT can help turn the calculation into a planner-reviewable decision board.

That matters because batch size can look like a clean calculation from the outside.

But in a real planning conversation, that number is only the first draft.

If the batch gets smaller, the business may carry less inventory and respond faster, but it may also create more setups, more changeovers, and more planning noise.

If the batch gets larger, the production run can look efficient because setup frequency drops, but the cost can come back later through trapped cash, shelf-life risk, slower response, or capacity used on the wrong product.

This is where ChatGPT becomes useful if we stop treating it like a calculator and start using it to build the first version of the decision artifact.

Give it the actual planning context: demand rate by SKU or family, setup or changeover cost, holding cost, current batch size, MOQ or pack-size rule, production rate, shelf life, capacity calendar, service priority, demand variability, and planner comments.

Then ask for a batch-size decision board.

The useful output is a review table that shows:
• first-pass EOQ
• smaller, current, and larger batch options
• setup or changeover burden
• inventory exposure
• capacity fit
• service risk
• assumptions that need to be verified 

Batch size decisions often hide behind the word efficiency. Bigger runs feel efficient because setup drops, but the planner still has to ask what the business is choosing to carry in return.

The value of AI here is not that it decides the perfect batch, the value is that it makes the trade-off visible before the planner changes the plan or master data.

If demand changed next week, would your team know which batch size is still carrying the right trade-off?

items.content:
Cooking dinner or ordering in is the same call companies make on everything they sell?

We're on procurement episode 32 at Shetty's Desk, and this is the decision that quietly shapes the whole business: do you make something yourself, or buy it from a supplier?

It feels like a price comparison, but it isn't. Two ideas sit underneath it. 

Transaction cost economics says make it in-house when dealing with the market is too costly or risky, and buy when the market does it cleanly. The core-competence view says keep what makes you different and outsource the rest.

So you weigh both sides on more than cost:
• Make gives you control and builds your own capability, but you carry the fixed cost and own every defect. 
• Buy rents a supplier's expertise and flexes with demand, but adds dependency and hands them the margin.

And the honest comparison is total cost of ownership, not the price per unit. The cheap quote that ties up your critical know-how can be the most expensive call you make.

To make this quite: buy what the market makes better and cheaper, and make what makes you, you.

Where have you outsourced something that turned out to be core?

items.content:
You don't need 50 metrics, you need 10 that map to SCOR's 5 performance attributes. Two per attribute - one for the boardroom, one for the floor. 

Most SC dashboards have the inverse: hundreds of operational numbers and almost nothing the CEO can actually use.

This is Episode 23 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 8 we covered SCOR as the universal supply chain language. Today we're using its five performance attributes as the structure for cutting a bloated KPI list down to the ten that actually matter.

The five SCOR attributes are: Reliability, Responsiveness, Agility, Cost, and Asset Management. For each attribute, you need two KPIs: one strategic (the boardroom number that tells leadership if you're healthy), and one operational (the floor number that tells the team what to act on today).

• Reliability:
Strategic: Perfect Order Rate (% of orders delivered complete, on time, undamaged, with correct documentation)
Operational: On-Time Delivery (% of orders shipped by promised date)

• Responsiveness:
Strategic: Order Fulfilment Cycle Time (average time from order to delivery)
Operational: Manufacturing Lead Time (production cycle time per unit)

• Agility:
Strategic: Upside Supply Chain Flexibility (% volume increase deliverable in 30 days)
Operational: Forecast Accuracy (forecast vs. actual at SKU level)

• Cost:
Strategic: Total Supply Chain Cost as % of Revenue
Operational: Cost per Order Shipped (or per unit)

• Asset Management:
Strategic: Cash-to-Cash Cycle Time (your CCC from Episode 22)
Operational: Inventory Turns (revenue / average inventory)

The mistake isn't picking the wrong metrics. It's reporting strategic metrics to the warehouse and operational metrics to the board. Both audiences need different numbers because they're solving different problems. Two scorecards, not one bigger one.

Which of these ten does your organisation track today, and how many of them actually shape decisions?

items.content:
Every procurement team has a process, although many never wrote it down. The ones that did outperform the ones that didn't.

This week on Supply Chain 101, Episode 29 we dive deep into the journey of a need to a PO.

There are seven steps between a sourcing need and a signed purchase order.
In a reactive team they run out of sequence, some get skipped entirely, and
the process rebuilds from scratch each time a new category comes up. In a
planned team the same seven steps run in order, and each one feeds the next.

• The foundation (Steps 1 to 3): Identify the real requirement, define
specifications clearly, and survey the supplier market before making contact
with anyone. These three steps take the most time, generate the most leverage downstream, and get cut most often when the team is under pressure.

• The market cycle (Steps 4 and 5): Issue the RFQ with the foundation complete and you get comparable, evaluable responses. Evaluate on total cost, lead time, and quality record, not price alone. A team that jumps to price at Step 5 undoes every hour invested in Steps 1 to 3.

• The close (Steps 6 and 7): Negotiate with a benchmark. Award and issue the PO with a written record of why this supplier was selected.

One of the key things that people miss out on: reactive purchasing and planned procurement use the same seven steps. The difference is whether your team reaches Step 3 before or after they have already committed to a supplier in their mind.

At which step does your procurement process most often stall?

items.content:
How does a list of 100 potential suppliers get down to the one who actually gets the order? 

Five filters. 

Most teams apply only one of them consistently.

This is Episode 27 of Supply Chain 101. We started the procurement series with scorecards to measure suppliers, then how a PO works. This is the process that decides which supplier earns a place on that PO.

The funnel has five stages:

• Market survey (100 → 20) Who even operates in this space? Capabilities, geography, certifications. Most teams rush this or skip it entirely, so the RFQ goes to suppliers who should not be receiving it.

• RFI qualified (20 → 8) Can you meet our minimum requirements? Lead time, financial stability, quality history. Suppliers who reach the RFQ have earned it.

• RFQ and evaluation (8 → 3) Price enters here, as one column in a scoring matrix, not as the entire decision.

• Shortlisted and awarded (3 → 1) Total cost, capability, risk, and the question most teams forget: can this supplier grow with us?

The parameter that a lot of people get stuck with is price. It is not the most critical one always, it is whether the supplier can scale with you. A supplier who matches your volume today but cannot in 18 months is a sourcing problem deferred, not solved.

At which stage in this funnel does your team consistently spend the least time?

---

items.content:
When strategic decisions get made with operational urgency, companies build warehouses they don't need. When operational decisions wait for strategic approval, customers don't get their orders. 

This is Episode 4 of Supply Chain 101. Last time we separated planning from scheduling. Today we're splitting planning itself into three layers, because treating them as one is where things start going sideways.

•  Strategic planning operates in years. It's about network design, market entry, and where to place capacity. The people in the room are the CEO, the VP of Supply Chain, and sometimes the board. These decisions shape everything downstream and they're expensive to reverse.

• Tactical planning operates in months to quarters. This is S&OP territory (which we'll cover in Episode 5). The question is: given the capacity we have, how do we allocate it across product lines and regions? Directors and senior managers own this layer, and the quality of their decisions depends entirely on whether the strategic layer above gave them clear guardrails.

• Operational planning operates in days to weeks. Which orders get prioritised? What do we produce on which line? This is where planners and schedulers live, and it's where most of the visible firefighting happens.


If you look a little closer, the problem isn't that companies don't plan. It's that they don't separate the layers. A five-year capacity question gets debated in a weekly operations meeting, or a daily prioritisation decision waits three weeks for a director's sign-off. Both cost money, both are avoidable.

Which level does your team spend the most time on? And is that actually where the biggest gap is?

---

items.content:
Why does everyone know which supplier is underperforming but nobody can prove it?

Because gut feel is not a scorecard, and without one, the conversation stays stuck at opinion.

Supplier scorecards are not about rating suppliers, they are about
what you weight. Score delivery at 30% and cost at 10%, and you
have just told your supplier team what this company actually values.
Most scorecards send the wrong message by accident.

This is Episode 25 of Supply Chain 101. From here, we go one function deep
per month. 

We start with procurement, because it sits at the
beginning of every supply chain and shapes everything that comes
after it.

A supplier scorecard gives you the one thing most procurement
conversations are missing: a number that everyone agreed on in
advance. Five criteria cover what actually matters:

• Quality is defect rate and spec compliance. It determines
 whether the product works. Most teams track this, but track it
 inconsistently because the threshold was never written down.

• Delivery is on-time-in-full against the date you needed it, not
 the date the supplier promised. Those two dates are often weeks
 apart, and measuring the wrong one masks the real performance.

• Cost is not unit price alone. It includes price stability,
 expediting charges, and rework costs that spread across four
 departments and never appear on the same report.

• Responsiveness is how fast they engage when something goes
 wrong. It is the most revealing criterion and the most skipped,
 because nobody thinks to score it until a crisis makes it obvious.

• Compliance is certifications, documentation, audit results. Low
 weight until it becomes the only weight.

The weighting row is the most important row in the scorecard.
A supplier scoring 74% overall can look acceptable until you
unpack it and find their delivery is flagged red. The total hides
what the breakdown exposes. What you weight is what you value,
and your suppliers will read that row before they read their score.

What would your most important supplier score today?

---

items.content:
Single-sourcing gives you leverage through volume. Multi-sourcing gives you resilience through options. 

The decision isn't about risk tolerance. It's about which risk you prefer to carry: the risk of dependency or the risk of complexity.

This is Episode 20 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 19 we covered JIT vs. JIC and the idea that inventory strategy should be segmented by product. Today we're applying that same logic to supplier strategy, because the number of suppliers you use for a category is one of the most consequential decisions in procurement, and most companies make it by default rather than by design.

• Single-sourcing means one supplier for a category. The advantages are real: concentrated volume gives you negotiating leverage, deeper relationships, simpler quality management, and often better pricing. The risk is equally real: if that supplier fails, you have no immediate alternative.

• Dual-sourcing means two suppliers sharing volume. It's the most common risk mitigation approach because it provides a built-in backup without excessive complexity. The trade-off is that neither supplier gets your full volume, which can dilute your leverage and may mean neither prioritises you as highly.

• Multi-sourcing means three or more suppliers. The advantage is maximum optionality and redundancy. The trade-off is significant management overhead: more contracts, more quality audits, more relationship management, and diluted volume across all of them.

Here's the thing most people miss: the number of suppliers matters less than three underlying factors. 
• Supply risk: how likely is disruption? 
• Spend volume: is there enough to split meaningfully? 
• And criticality: what happens if this component is unavailable? 

A low-risk, high-volume commodity might be fine with a single source. A high-risk, critical component with limited alternatives needs at least two, and they should not be in the same geography.

For your top 5 spend categories, can you name a tested alternative?

items.content:
A 5% increase in consumer demand can become a 40% spike at the raw material supplier!?!

Each link in the chain over-orders to protect itself, and the further upstream you go, the wilder the swings get. This has had a name since 1961 and most supply chains today are struggling to solve for it.

This is Episode 11 of Supply Chain 101. We're following the mechanics of how supply chains operate. Today's concept is the bullwhip effect, and once you see it, you'll recognise it everywhere.

Procter & Gamble first documented this with Pampers nappies. Retail sales were remarkably stable, but upstream orders were swinging wildly. The supply chain was reacting to orders, not to demand, and the gap between those two things is where the bullwhip lives.

There are four root causes, and they all share a common thread:
• Demand signal processing: each tier forecasts from orders, not actual demand
• Order batching: companies order in bulk at intervals rather than continuously
• Price fluctuations: promotions and discounts create artificial demand spikes
• Rationing and shortage gaming: when supply is tight, buyers inflate orders to secure allocation

What I believe is that this isn't a forecasting problem. It's an information-sharing problem. The fix isn't better algorithms. It's making actual demand data visible further upstream so every tier works from the same signal instead of amplifying it.

How many tiers up does your actual demand data travel?

items.content:
How does a car manufacturer decide to build 50,000 vehicles before a single buyer walks into a dealership? And why would a yacht builder refuse to start without a signed contract and a custom specification? 
The answer is the production strategy.

This is Episode 7 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 6 we covered push vs. pull and the decoupling point. Today we're zooming in on what that looks like in practice, because the production strategy is essentially where your company has placed that line.

There are three main strategies, and the simplest way to understand them is by asking: where does the customer order enter the process?

• Make to Stock (MTS) means you produce finished goods before any customer order exists. The product sits on a shelf or in a warehouse, ready to ship. Think cereal, toothpaste, or IKEA furniture. The advantage is immediate availability. The risk is that you're betting your forecast is right, and when it isn't, you're sitting on inventory nobody wants.

• Make to Order (MTO) means production only starts after a customer places an order. Think custom furniture, industrial equipment, or a Dell laptop circa 2005. The advantage is no finished goods inventory and a product tailored to the order. The trade-off is a longer lead time that the customer has to accept.

• Engineer to Order (ETO) means even the design doesn't start until the customer commits. Think Boeing aircraft, offshore oil platforms, or bespoke machinery. The advantage is a product built exactly to specification. The reality is lead times measured in months or years and a supply chain built entirely around project management.

Here's the thing most people miss: the mistake isn't choosing the wrong strategy. It's running one strategy across an entire portfolio when different product lines need different approaches. Your commodity products and your custom products should not be on the same planning logic.

Which strategy does your highest-margin product line use? And was that a deliberate choice?

---

items.content:
A 1PL owns every truck and every warehouse whereas a 5PL owns nothing and manages everything. The further up the ladder you go, the less you physically control and the more you strategically coordinate. 

This is Episode 16 of Supply Chain 101. We've covered how supply chains buy, hold inventory, manage cost, and classify complexity. Today we're closing with how goods actually move, and specifically how companies decide who moves them.

There are five levels of logistics outsourcing, and each one represents a different trade-off between control and capability:
• 1PL: you do everything yourself. Own trucks, own warehouses, own drivers. Think of a local brewery delivering its own beer. Maximum control, but it only scales if logistics is your core business.
• 2PL: you outsource transport to a carrier or freight forwarder. They move your goods, but you manage the rest. This is the most basic form of outsourcing.
• 3PL: you outsource warehousing, transport, and fulfilment to a logistics provider. They handle operations on your behalf. This is where most mid-to-large companies sit today, and it's the level most people mean when they say "we use a logistics partner."
• 4PL: you bring in a partner that doesn't just operate. They manage your other logistics providers, optimise routes, and coordinate across the network. A 4PL is a strategist, not a truck operator.
• 5PL: the entire logistics function is managed as a platform or network service. Think large e-commerce platforms that orchestrate thousands of carriers, warehouses, and fulfilment centres through technology. This is logistics as a managed ecosystem.

The decision point isn't which level sounds most impressive. It's when your complexity outgrows your team's ability to coordinate, and that's the signal to move up.

What level does your logistics operation actually require?

items.content:
Safety stock exists because the future is uncertain. But most companies calculate it using averages, which assume the future behaves like the past. The very thing safety stock is meant to protect against is the thing the formula ignores.

This is Episode 12 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 11 we covered the bullwhip effect and how demand signals distort as they move upstream. Today we're looking at one of the most direct consequences of that distortion: how much extra inventory you keep as a buffer.

Safety stock is the cushion between your expected demand and reality. When your supplier delivers late, or demand spikes unexpectedly, safety stock is what keeps the customer from waiting. 

It sits below your regular inventory (called cycle stock) and above zero, and ideally you never touch it. But it's there so the business doesn't stop when something goes wrong.

The calculation depends on three variables:
• Demand variability: how much does customer demand fluctuate?
• Supply variability: how reliable are your supplier lead times?
• Service level target: what percentage of orders do you want to fulfil from stock?

If demand is stable and your supplier is reliable, you need less safety stock. If either one is volatile, you need more. And if your target service level is 99% instead of 95%, the buffer increases significantly, because that last 4% is expensive.

What most people do not realise is that reducing lead time variability is a better lever than tweaking the safety stock formula. A supplier that always delivers in 10 days needs less buffer than one that averages 10 days but swings between 7 and 15. 

When did you last recalculate your safety stock parameters?

items.content:
20% of your SKUs drive 80% of your revenue. That's the Pareto principle, and most supply chain teams know it. But revenue alone doesn't tell you how to plan them from an SC perspective. It is the second dimension, demand predictability, that changes everything.

This is Episode 14 of Supply Chain 101. In Episodes 12 and 13 we covered safety stock and lead time. Today we're looking at how you decide which SKUs deserve the most planning attention in the first place, because treating 10,000 SKUs the same way is how planners burn out and inventory gets misallocated.

ABC classification sorts your SKUs by value contribution:
• A items: the top 20% of SKUs that drive roughly 80% of revenue
• B items: the next 30% contributing around 15%
• C items: the bottom 50% contributing the remaining 5%
That's useful, but it only tells you what matters financially. It doesn't tell you how to plan it. That's where XYZ comes in.

XYZ classification sorts by demand predictability:
• X items: stable, predictable demand (low forecast error)
• Y items: some variability, often seasonal or trend-driven
• Z items: erratic, unpredictable, hard to forecast

Combine the two into a 3x3 matrix, and suddenly the planning approach becomes obvious:
• AX (high value, stable demand): automate replenishment, minimal manual intervention
• AZ (high value, erratic demand): your planner's full attention, manual review, tighter safety stock monitoring
• CZ (low value, erratic demand): seriously consider whether these should still be in your catalogue

The matrix doesn't just classify inventory. It classifies where human effort should go. And in most organisations, that effort is spread evenly when it should be concentrated.

How many SKUs fall in your CZ box, and does anyone review them?

items.content:
When demand moves, the first question should not be “who was wrong?”

That sounds obvious, but it happens more often than people admit.

The team explains the variance, the baseline was too high, a promotion did not lift the way it was expected to, orders moved between weeks, a customer pulled back.

All of that is useful, but it is still only the diagnostic layer.

The real value starts when the team asks what the miss changes.
Does inventory need to move? Does capacity need to shift? Does supply need to be expedited, delayed, or rebalanced? Does the customer promise still hold?

This is where demand planning becomes more than a forecast review. The forecast is an input, but the demand plan is the operating commitment the business chooses to make after looking at the signal, the assumption, the risk, and the trade-off.

A stronger demand review separates four things very clearly:
• what signal changed
• where the forecast missed
• which assumption needs to be tested
• which decision changes next

And if the same miss keeps coming back, the answer is not always to tune the model harder. Sometimes the team needs to update the assumption the model is built around.

That is the idea behind this decision lens: read the miss, test the assumption, and then change the decision with discipline.

If actual demand moved away from the forecast tomorrow, which decision would your team change first?

items.content:
Why does IKEA build millions of bookshelves before anyone orders one, while Dell used to wait for your exact configuration before assembling a single laptop? 

Both were right. The difference is where each company draws the line.

This is Episode 6 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 5 we covered S&OP and how companies align sales ambition with operational reality. 

Today we're looking at the fundamental design choice underneath all of that: do you make before the customer asks, or after?

• A push supply chain produces based on what it expects to sell. Raw materials are ordered, products are manufactured, and inventory is moved into warehouses and stores before a single customer order exists. The upside is speed to the customer. The risk is overstock, markdowns, and waste when the forecast is wrong.

• A pull supply chain waits for actual demand. Nothing moves until a customer places an order. The upside is that you only build what's been bought. The risk is longer lead times and the possibility that customers won't wait.

But here's what makes this more interesting than a simple either/or: most supply chains are hybrid. They push up to a certain point (raw materials, components, semi-finished goods) and pull from that point forward (final assembly, customisation, delivery). 

That boundary is called the decoupling point, and where you place it determines your inventory, your lead time, and your responsiveness.

• Moving the decoupling point upstream makes you more responsive but requires better demand visibility.
• Moving it downstream makes you more efficient but slower to react. 

There's no universal right answer, only a right answer for your product, your customer, and your market. Where does the decoupling point sit in your supply chain? And did someone choose it, or did it just end up there?

---

items.content:
Why did some companies recover from 2020–2025 disruptions in weeks while others took years? 

Not because they predicted the events. Because they had categorised the risks, and the framework told them where to look first.

This is Episode 21 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 20 we covered sourcing strategy and the trade-offs between single, dual, and multi-source. Today we're zooming out to look at the broader question: how do you systematically think about everything that could go wrong, without trying to predict the unpredictable?

The starting point is a 2x2 risk matrix: probability on one axis, impact on the other. Every potential disruption gets plotted. 

Within that matrix, supply chain risks tend to fall into five categories:
• Geopolitical: trade wars, sanctions, regional conflicts, regulatory changes
• Supplier: financial collapse, capacity loss, quality failure, single-point-of-failure
• Demand: sudden shifts, customer concentration, market collapse
• Operational: cyberattacks, IT failures, labour disruption, internal capacity loss
• External: pandemics, climate events, infrastructure failures, currency shocks

Here's what's important to remember: you don't need to predict the next pandemic, the next ship-stuck-in-a-canal, or the next regional conflict. You need to know which of these five categories your operation is most exposed to right now, and have a documented response for each. The framework isn't a crystal ball. It's a map of where to look first when something changes.

The two levers that consistently separate companies that recover from those that struggle are visibility (do you know what's happening upstream and downstream as it unfolds?) and optionality (do you have alternatives ready, or do you have to scramble to find them?).

Does your supply chain have a documented risk register?

items.content:
You can be 10 years deep into supply chain and still not know which career you're actually building? 

A lot of paths share the same three letters at the entry level, although they diverge fast after that.

This is Episode 24 of Supply Chain 101. Over the past 23 episodes we've covered the language, the mechanics, and the strategy of supply chain. Today we're breaking down the question almost everyone in the field eventually asks: where can I actually go from here?

Supply chain is not a single and linear career path. It's at least six, branching from a common entry point into completely different executive destinations. Each path requires a different mix of skills, attracts a different temperament, and leads somewhere recognisably distinct.

• Procurement: deep in supplier relationships, negotiation, total cost analysis, category strategy -> leads to CPO or VP of Sourcing.

• Planning and S&OP: forecasting, demand-supply balancing, capacity allocation, integrated business planning -> leads to VP of Supply Chain or Chief Supply Chain Officer.

• Logistics: warehousing, transportation, distribution, network design, 3PL/4PL management -> Path leads to Head of Operations or VP of Logistics.

• Manufacturing: production, quality, lean, capacity, plant management -> Path leads to COO or VP of Operations.

• Analytics and digital: forecasting models, optimisation, control towers, data infrastructure, AI applications -> leads to Chief Data Officer or Chief Digital Officer.

• Strategy and consulting: network design, transformation, M&A integration, advisory -> leads to Chief Strategy Officer, partner-track consulting, or independent advisory.

What you need to consider is that the highest-impact supply chain leaders are T-shaped, not I-shaped. They go deep in one path, but they're literate across all six. They can speak procurement to a CPO, planning to a CSCO, and analytics to a CDO without translation. That breadth is what gets them invited into rooms specialists never reach.

If you've followed the series from the start, you've now seen the language, the mechanics, and the strategy. The career map is what ties them together. Each of the 23 concepts we covered maps more naturally to one or two of these six paths than the others. 

Which paths spoke to you?

Which path are you on, and which adjacent path would make you the most valuable version of yourself in five years?

---

A standard RFQ takes 2 to 3 days to write internally. With a structured Claude prompt and your requirements pasted in, it takes 20 minutes. 

The difference is not quality, it is knowing which inputs to prepare before you open the chat.

Supply Chain 101 covered the procurement funnel this week. This is the execution layer: the same process, with a tool that cuts RFQ writing.

Most procurement teams rebuild the same document structure every time they go to market. The scope section, the technical requirements, the commercial terms and the evaluation criteria. None of these change dramatically between categories, and yet they get rewritten from scratch, reviewed internally, revised for language, and sent out three days later than they needed to be.

The prompt that cuts this to 20 minutes has five inputs; that is the preparation work. Everything else Claude handles.

• Category -> What you are sourcing, approximate annual volume, and the number of suppliers you plan to invite.

• Specifications -> Your technical requirements. Paste in whatever you have: a product brief, a spec sheet summary, even a bullet list. Claude structures it.

• Scoring Criteria -> How you will evaluate responses. Quality, price, lead time, references. You decide the weighting. Claude writes the scoring matrix.

• Commercial terms  -> Payment terms, Incoterms, contract length expectation.

• Timeline -> When you need supplier responses and when you plan to award.

Then paste the prompt in the comments into Claude. 

The output is a complete RFQ. Review the requirements as those are yours to own whereas the structure and language are Claude's.

One caveat: if your input data is incomplete or your specifications are still a rough list, the document structure will be clean but the requirements inside it will still need your work. Claude builds around what you give it.

items.content:
Why did your company choose the cheapest supplier and end up spending more? 

This is Episode 15 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 14 we covered how to classify SKUs by value and demand pattern. Today we're looking at how companies evaluate what they pay for those SKUs, because the number on the purchase order is only the tip of the iceberg.

Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) is what you actually pay when you account for everything beyond unit price. 

Think of it as an iceberg:
Above the waterline is the unit price. It's visible, it's on the quote, and it's what most procurement negotiations focus on.

Below the waterline is everything else:
• Transport and customs: freight, duties, insurance
• Quality costs: inspections, rejects, rework, returns
• Inventory carrying: safety stock buffers driven by lead time variability
• Administrative overhead: supplier management, communication, expediting
• Lead time costs: the cash tied up while goods are in transit or in buffer
• Payment terms: the financial impact of when you actually pay

In most cases, the below-waterline costs are 2–3x larger than the unit price itself. And they're spread across different departments (logistics, quality, finance, planning) so nobody connects them back to the original sourcing decision.

What often happens is in practice the supplier that's 15% cheaper on unit price is picked but has 3x longer lead times requires significantly more safety stock. That inventory costs money to hold, ties up working capital, and carries obsolescence risk. Run the full TCO calculation and the saving often disappears.

Does your procurement team evaluate on unit price or total cost?

---

items.content:
Why the sentence "can you just change the plan?" is rarely as simple as it sounds? 

Sales may see demand, finance may see revenue, customer service may see a promise date. 

But operations has to translate that into lines, people, materials, tooling, changeovers, quality checks, supplier arrivals, and all the smaller constraints that do not show up neatly when the number first changes.

That is where the production plan sits.

It is the translation layer between demand ambition and factory commitment, it takes the demand signal and asks a more grounded set of questions:
• Do we have the capacity?
• Do we have the material?
• Do we have the labor and skills?
• What does the sequence do to changeover?
• What gets delayed if we pull this forward?
• Is this still a plan, or has it become a fire drill?

The factory schedule is more detailed. It says what runs on which line, in which sequence, and when.

The production plan comes before that. It decides what the factory should commit to build across the planning horizon after the constraints have been checked.

Sometimes the answer is yes. Sometimes the answer is yes, but with a service, cost, overtime, inventory, or changeover trade-off. And sometimes the honest answer is no, because the constraint moved faster than the plan could absorb.

A good production plan does not make the factory rigid. It makes the trade-offs visible early enough for the business to make a better decision.

When demand changes, which constraint changes the plan first in your 
environment?

One 2x2 grid, drawn in 1983, still decides how the best buyers spend their time.

This month on Shetty's Desk we're on procurement; in episode 31 we dig underneath comparing quotes sits a bigger idea: you can't manage every supplier the same way.

In 1983, Peter Kraljic drew a simple 2x2 in Harvard Business Review. 

Plot everything you buy on two questions, how much it moves your profit and how hard it is to source, and where it lands tells you how to behave:
• Leverage items are big spend but easy to find, so you make suppliers compete on price. 
• Strategic items are critical and hard to replace, so you build the relationship and protect it. 
• Bottleneck items are cheap but single-source, so the job is to secure supply before it bites. 
• Routine items are the small stuff, so you automate them and stop spending attention there.

The common instinct is to negotiate hardest where it's easy. The matrix tells you to put your energy where both the stakes and the risk are high. Which of your suppliers are you treating as routine when they're quietly strategic?

items.content:
A PO is not a document. It is a legal commitment, a finance record, and a supplier instruction all at once.

Treating it as a form to fill in is how approvals get missed, invoices get disputed, and payments run 60 days late.
 
This is Episode 26 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 25 we started the Procurement month with the supplier scorecard. Today we follow the purchase order from the moment a need is identified to the moment the invoice is paid, because most of the friction in procurement-finance relationships lives somewhere in these seven steps.

And it moves through seven hands before it closes:

• Requisition: someone in the business identifies a need and raises a formal request. This is where the process starts andd where most ad-hoc buying bypasses the system entirely.

• Approval: the requisition goes through an authorisation workflow. The delay here is almost always process, not urgency. Most approvals take longer than the actual purchase.

• PO creation: procurement converts the approved requisition into a legal purchase order and sends it to the supplier. At this point the company has made a financial commitment.

• Supplier confirmation: the supplier acknowledges receipt and confirms they can fulfil the order. Without this, you have a commitment with no confirmation it will be met.

• Goods receipt: the warehouse records what was actually received. This step is the one most often done late, informally, or not at all, and it is what makes the next step possible.

• Invoice matching: finance matches the supplier invoice against the PO and the goods receipt note. This is the three-way match, and it is where most payment delays originate. If goods receipt was never recorded, the match cannot close.

• Payment: the invoice is approved and payment is released to the supplier.

The gap between goods receipt and invoice matching is where most SC-finance friction lives. Not because the process is wrong, but because two teams own adjacent steps and rarely communicate when one step is late.

How many of these seven steps does your team own end-to-end?

items.content:
Just-in-Time was the greatest supply chain innovation of the 20th century. Just-in-Case was the lesson of 2020. 

This is Episode 19 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 18 we covered the nearshoring decision and total landed cost. Today we're looking at one of the most misunderstood debates in supply chain: should you run lean or should you hold buffer?

• Just-in-Time (JIT) is an inventory philosophy that originated at Toyota. The idea is simple: materials arrive exactly when they're needed in production, not before. The benefit is minimal waste, lower inventory costs, and a faster, more responsive operation. But it requires extremely reliable suppliers, consistent quality, short replenishment cycles, and stable demand. When those conditions exist, JIT is powerful. When they don't, it's fragile.

• Just-in-Case (JIC) is the opposite instinct: hold enough inventory to absorb disruption. The benefit is resilience. The cost is tied-up capital, warehouse space, and the risk of obsolescence. After 2020, many companies swung hard toward JIC, adding weeks or months of buffer stock across their entire portfolio.

But here's what makes this more nuanced than a binary choice: the right approach depends on the product. 

• A high-value, critical component with a single supplier in a volatile region probably needs a JIC buffer. 
• A low-cost, widely available commodity with three local suppliers can run JIT safely.

My view on this is that the mature answer is portfolio segmentation. Not every product line needs the same inventory strategy. The companies that segment, applying JIT where conditions support it and JIC where the risk demands it, are managing cost and resilience simultaneously rather than trading one for the other.

Which items in your supply chain run JIT by default rather than by design?

items.content:
Supply chain leaders who can't talk in O2C and P2P language get treated as operators, not strategists. The decisions you make every day (lead times, inventory, supplier terms) directly drive the metric your CFO actually cares about: cash conversion.

This is Episode 22 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 21 we covered risk management. Today we're connecting supply chain to the two financial cycles that determine how cash actually flows through the business, because every decision you make about lead times, inventory, and supplier terms is shaping these cycles whether you realise it or not.

• Order-to-Cash (O2C) is the cycle from the moment a customer places an order to the moment the cash hits your bank account. It includes order management, fulfilment, invoicing, and collection. The metric that summarises it is Days Sales Outstanding (DSO): on average, how many days does it take to collect payment after a sale? Lower is better.

• Procure-to-Pay (P2P) is the mirror image. It runs from the moment you identify a need to buy something, through purchasing, receipt, invoice approval, and payment to the supplier.  The metric is Days Payable Outstanding (DPO): on average, how many days do you take to pay after receiving goods? Higher (within reason) is better for cash flow.

The gap between these two, plus the time inventory sits in between, is the Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC). DSO + Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO) - DPO = CCC. It's the metric your CFO actually watches, and it's almost entirely shaped by supply chain decisions: how much inventory you hold, how fast you fulfil orders, what payment terms you negotiate.

Supply chain leaders who frame their work in CCC terms get heard in the boardroom. The same decisions, framed as service levels or fill rates, sound operational. Framed as working capital impact, they sound strategic.

Can you calculate your company's CCC?

items.content:
Sales says we'll sell 10,000 units. Operations says we can make 7,000. Finance has budgeted for 8,500. Somebody has to be wrong. S&OP is the process that figures out who, and what to do about it.

Today, we're onto Episode 5 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 4 we covered the three levels of planning. S&OP lives in the tactical layer, and it's probably the most talked-about process in supply chain that is also the most inconsistently executed.

S&OP stands for Sales and Operations Planning. It's a monthly cycle with five steps, and each one has a specific purpose:

• Demand Review is where the commercial side presents its forecast. What do we expect to sell, where, and when? 
• Supply Review is where operations responds with what's actually possible given current capacity, materials, and constraints. 
• Pre-S&OP is where the gaps between those two get surfaced and options are prepared. 
• Executive S&OP is where leadership makes the trade-off decisions (do we add a shift, delay a launch, or accept the shortfall?). 
• Implementation is where those decisions get translated into the operational and financial plans that everyone works from.

Here's the thing most people miss: the meeting itself is maybe 30% of the value. The other 70% comes from the preparation between meetings and the accountability that follows. Companies that treat S&OP as a monthly slide deck get monthly slide deck results. Companies that treat it as a decision-making rhythm get aligned execution.

Does your S&OP change behaviour, or is it a monthly PowerPoint ritual?

items.content:
In under 2 seconds, 22 humans execute 80 coordinated actions to swap all four tires on a car.  Red Bull's pit crew practices the same 1.8-second sequence over 1,000 times between races. 

Most operations leaders assume more hands on a task means more coordination chaos. F1 proved the opposite, the difference is one word: parallel process.

• The 70-year curve: F1 pit stops fell from 67 seconds in 1950 to 1.80 seconds in 2023, a 97% reduction achieved without adding a single robotic arm.

• The architecture shift: 22 crew members execute over 80 actions simultaneously because each wheel station runs 3 dedicated roles in parallel, making total time equal to the slowest corner, not the sum of all four.

• The hidden blocker: Most SMED projects stall at 40% improvement because the cost of serial changeover design is buried in OEE spreadsheets, while F1 teams can price every lost tenth of a second in championship prize money north of $100K.

I believe that the biggest changeover gains in manufacturing aren't locked behind capital equipment budgets. They're locked behind the assumption that one technician working a sequential checklist is 'lean' when it's actually the most expensive process architecture you can run.

When was the last time your organisation mapped a changeover not by step duration, but by how many steps are sitting idle waiting their turn?

items.content:
Why does your supplier say 6 weeks but the customer waits 10? Because supplier lead time is one of at least five lead times in your supply chain, and it's the only a portion most companies measure.

This is Episode 13 of Supply Chain 101. In Episode 12 we covered safety stock and how lead time variability drives how much buffer you need. Today we're unpacking lead time itself, because most companies are only measuring a fraction of it.

When someone says "lead time," they usually mean supplier lead time: how long it takes from placing a PO to receiving the goods. But that's one segment of a much longer chain.

The full cumulative lead time breaks down into at least five components:
• Information lead time: how long it takes to identify the need, get approval, and enter the order into the system. This is pure decision speed, and it's often invisible.
• Supplier lead time: how long the supplier takes to produce or ship the goods after receiving the order.
• Manufacturing lead time: if you're transforming what you receive, how long does your own production take?
• Transportation lead time: time in transit from supplier to your facility, or from your facility to the customer.
• Receiving and QC lead time: time to unload, inspect, check quality, and make goods available in the system.

Add those up and you get the real lead time. In most cases I've seen, supplier lead time is less than half the total. 

While cutting 3 days of information lead time (faster decisions, fewer approval loops) often costs nothing. Cutting 3 days of transportation lead time might mean airfreight or a completely different logistics network. 


Have you mapped the full cumulative lead time for your top 10 SKUs?

The answer to a bad forecast isn't a better forecast. It's recognising that forecasting was never meant to be the only tool. 

This is Episode 17 of Supply Chain 101. We're now moving into the Strategy of supply chains. We've covered the language and the mechanics. Now we're looking at the decisions that separate average supply chains from competitive advantages. 

And it starts with demand, because everything in a supply chain flows from what customers want, when they want it, and whether you can influence either.

• Demand planning is what most people mean when they say "forecasting." It uses historical data, market intelligence, and statistical models to predict what customers will buy months from now. It's essential, and it's also inherently limited, because the further out you look, the less accurate it gets. A 60-75% accuracy rate is considered normal, and that remaining 25-40% is where most supply chain pain comes from.

• Demand sensing is the short-term correction. It uses real-time signals (point-of-sale data, web traffic, order patterns, weather, events) to detect what's actually happening right now, not what the model predicted three months ago. It operates in days to weeks and typically achieves 80-90% accuracy because it's working with current information rather than projections.

• Demand shaping is the most underused of the three. Instead of predicting or detecting demand, it actively influences it. Pricing changes, promotions, product bundling, substitution offers, allocation decisions. Airlines do this constantly: dynamic pricing is demand shaping in its purest form.

My view on this is that most supply chains treat demand as something to predict rather than something to manage. Planning, sensing, and shaping aren't alternatives. They're layers, and the companies that run all three are working with a fundamentally different demand picture.

Does your supply chain team have a seat at the table when pricing decisions are made?

items.content:
Why does every cost reduction programme start with a conversation and end with a spreadsheet nobody agrees on?

We started with a need to PO journey on Supply Chain 101, earlier this week. Now we jump into Episode 30.

A spend analysis maps all organisational spend by supplier, category, and
business unit to show where the money actually goes. It is not a cost
reduction programme. It is the picture that makes one possible.

The Pareto principle holds across almost every organisation that has run a
proper spend analysis. Twenty percent of spend categories account for eighty percent of total spend. 

The strategic categories are usually visible because someone manages them. The problem is the tail: fragmented spend across dozens of smaller categories where no one has clear ownership and the per-unit cost is consistently higher than it needs to be.

• Direct spend is usually managed: Someone negotiates the materials that go
into the product, tracks the suppliers, and monitors performance. The data is
imperfect but the visibility exists.

• Indirect spend is a different story: Facilities, IT, professional services,
travel, MRO. In most organisations this runs between 15 and 30% of revenue.
Almost none of it is managed strategically because no one has mapped what is actually being spent and with whom.

My view on this is that cost reduction programmes stall not because the
savings are not there, but because the spend is not visible enough to know
where to start. A spend analysis does not find the savings, it finds the
categories where savings are most likely to exist.

Does your team know which category holds the most unmanaged spend in your organisation right now?

There are over 250 supply chain metrics in common use. SCOR organises them into 6 processes and 5 performance attributes. It's the closest thing supply chain has to a universal language, and it's been around since 1996.

This is Episode 8 of Supply Chain 101. We've spent the last few episodes building up the vocabulary of how supply chains plan, produce, and respond to demand. Today we're stepping back and looking at the whole picture, because SCOR is the framework that ties all of it together.

SCOR stands for Supply Chain Operations Reference. 
It was developed in 1996 and it does something deceptively simple: it says every supply chain on earth, regardless of industry, performs the same six processes.
• Plan sits at the centre. It's the process that balances demand and supply and coordinates everything else 
• Source is how you acquire what you need
• Make is how you transform it
• Deliver is how you get it to the customer
• Return handles anything that comes back 
• Enable is the foundation underneath all five: the rules, data, technology, and people that keep the system running

On the measurement side, SCOR gives you five performance attributes to evaluate how well those processes work: 
• Reliability (do you deliver what you promised?)
• Responsiveness (how fast?)
• Agility (can you flex when things change?)
• Cost (what does it cost to operate?)
• Asset Management (how efficiently do you use what you have?)

SCOR is misunderstood only as an academic exercise, but it's more of a benchmarking tool. 

A supply chain manager at a food company and one at an electronics firm can compare reliability scores because the definitions are standardised. That comparability is what makes it powerful, and it's what most internal KPI dashboards lack.

If you had to pick one of those five attributes your company is weakest on, which would it be?
